data.title: Preprint: Model-guided placement of decentralized diagnostics for spatial control of the 2026 Bundibugyo Ebola epidemic
data.authors: Klein, D. J.; Grantz, K. H.; Buckee, C. O.; George, D. B.; Dowell, S. F.
data.abstract: Before 2026, Bundibugyo virus disease had only two recognized outbreaks. By August 2026, delayed recognition and multi-day sample transport in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo had contributed to a large, spatially dispersed epidemic. We hypothesized that model-guided placement of decentralized diagnostics in frontier health zones could help contain spatial spread by acting as a spatial fence: delayed recognition would be converted into timely polymerase chain reaction (PCR) confirmation, isolation, and contact tracing before imported lineages became established. We fit a Bayesian spatial branching process to public situation reports through 2 August 2026, with Flowminder movement and a latent-burden anchor. Lineages had overdispersed offspring, PCR access and turnaround, clinical recognition, isolation, tracing, safe burial, and local behaviour change. Because the observed history did not identify future control, we assumed a national response ramp yielding West-Africa-scale status-quo burden and replayed 2,000 posterior trees with 5-100 zone-level PCR laboratories, deployment delays of 0-180 days, and postmortem rapid diagnostic test (RDT) coverage. The posterior reproduced case, death, latent-burden, and spatial targets. Speed dominated: 35 PCR laboratories averted a median 49% of future deaths if deployed immediately, 38% after 14 days, and 11% after 60 days, with 90% prediction intervals of 30-65%, 23-53%, and 5-20%, respectively. Placement also mattered: with a 30-day delay, model-informed placement averted 18-33% of future deaths with 20-100 laboratories, versus 1-8% under random placement. Postmortem RDTs partly filled gaps left by live-case detection, increasing future deaths averted from 26% to 41% with 20 laboratories, a 14-day delay, and 75% coverage. Decentralized diagnostics can slow spatial spread when they are placed ahead of likely importations and paired with staffing, isolation, tracing, and safe-burial capacity.

data.title: Preprint: Estimating Hepatitis C Virus Prevalence in US States and the District of Columbia, 2017-2020
data.authors: Bradley, H.; Yu, Y.-H.; Li, L.; Kapadia, S. N.; Sullivan, P. S.; Hall, E. W.
data.abstract: Background State-level estimates of hepatitis C virus (HCV) prevalence are needed to guide resource allocation and to provide a baseline against which to measure progress toward elimination goals. Population prevalence is not directly observable, requiring estimation from indirect data sources. Methods We adapted a Bayesian spatial integrated abundance model to estimate state-level HCV prevalence during 2017-2020 across 48 states and the District of Columbia. The model integrated six HCV-related outcomes: acute and chronic surveillance cases, HCV-related deaths, observations of HCV in [MarketScan] administrative claims data, diagnoses of HCV in Medicaid recipients, and treatment with direct-acting antivirals in Medicaid recipients. Estimates were anchored to a national prevalence estimate, and the model accounted for data source-specific selection, heterogeneity in HCV risk factors across states, and geospatial correlation. Results Estimated average prevalence was 1.32% (95% credible interval [CrI]: 0.94%-1.80%), corresponding to 3.33 million (95% CrI: 2.37-4.65 million) adults with HCV infection across 48 states and DC. State estimates ranged from 0.74% in North Dakota to 2.22% in Oklahoma (median state-specific prevalence, 1.27%), with higher prevalence concentrated in South Central states, Appalachia, and the West, and the lower prevalence in the upper Midwest, Southeast, and New England. Ten states accounted for 56% of estimated infections. Estimates were stable in sensitivity analyses (most differences <1 percentage point). The model integrated six HCV-related outcomes: acute and chronic surveillance cases, HCV-related deaths, observations of HCV in [MarketScan] administrative claims data, diagnoses of HCV in Medicaid recipients, and treatment with direct-acting antivirals in Medicaid recipients. Estimates were anchored to a national prevalence estimate, and the model accounted for data source-specific selection, heterogeneity in HCV risk factors across states, and geospatial correlation. data.title: Preprint: Sample Size and Power Calculations Based on Endpoint Responsiveness: Applications to Trials of Disease-Modifying Therapies in Parkinson's Disease
data.authors: Pedrera Gomez, M.; Bernasconi, C.; Mazza, C.; Belachew, S.
data.abstract: In Parkinson's disease (PD), early phase clinical trials of disease-modifying agents generally use the MDS-UPDRS Part III as the primary outcome measure of motor function, which typically requires a large sample and/or a long (12-18 months) treatment duration, even if a substantial treatment effect is assumed. This is due to the rather slow rate of early PD progression relative to the variability of the MDS-UPDRS Part III assessments. Using placebo-arm data from four recent large Phase 2 trials of early-stage PD (SPARK, PASADENA, PADOVA and LUMA), the sample size needed to detect a range of assumed treatment effects on MDS-UPDRS Part III progression was estimated. The trial sample size estimates obtained for MDS-UPDRS Part III and for smartphone-based sensor-derived motor functional composite (MFC) endpoints were compared using an approach based on relative responsiveness to disease progression. The calculations were also implemented in an interactive, publicly accessible application. Powering a one-year trial using the MFC1 endpoint, derived from three active assessments (6-minute walk, U-turn and Hand Pronation-Supination), or the MFC2, which adds 60-Second Typing, was projected to reduce the required sample size by more than half relative to the MDS-UPDRS Part III, assuming equivalent proportional treatment effects.

data.title: Preprint: Distinct Sex-Associated Phenotypes of Sudden Cardiac Arrest Across Clinical, ECG, and Echocardiographic Domains: Replication in Two Communities and Comparison with the Framingham Heart Study
data.authors: Truyen, T. T. T. T.; Chugh, H.; Nguyen, D.; Nakamura, K.; Uy-Evanado, A.; Benjamin, E. J.; Reinier, K.; Chugh, S. S.
data.abstract: Background: Sex differences in sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) incidence and outcomes are well established, but risk stratification underperforms in women. It is important to delineate sex-specific patterns in SCA across clinical, electrocardiographic, and echocardiographic domains. Methods: We studied out-of-hospital SCA cases from the Oregon Sudden Unexpected Death Study (ORSUDS; Portland, 2002-2020; discovery) and Prediction of Sudden Death in Multi-Ethnic Communities (PRESTO; Ventura County, 2015-2024; external replication). Sex differences in 38 comorbidities, 19 ECG and 12 echocardiographic measures were estimated using multivariable-adjusted logistic regression. Female sex was the modeled dependent measure (male as reference). ORSUDS estimates were compared with those in the Framingham Heart Study (FHS), a community-based reference cohort, using FDR-adjusted Cochran Q tests. Results: Among 5130 ORSUDS cases, 1715 (33.4%) were women (median age, 70.4 years [IQR, 58.7-81.8]) and 3415 (66.6%) were men (65.6 [55.0-76.8]). Compared with men, women had higher BMI (per 5 kg/m2, 1.11 [1.08-1.15]) and higher odds of thyroid disease (2.56 [2.17-3.13]), asthma (2.33 [1.92-2.86]), mood disorder (2.17 [1.85-2.50]), dementia (1.27 [1.02-1.56]), and left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH, 3.13 [2.44-4.00]). Women also had lower odds of coronary artery disease (0.61 [0.52-0.71]), atrial fibrillation (0.67 [0.56-0.79]), prolonged QTc (0.45 [0.35-0.57]), prolonged PR (0.53 [0.41-0.68]), premature contractions (0.77 [0.60-0.98]), sleep apnea (0.53 [0.43-0.65]), and reduced LVEF (0.40 [0.29-0.54]). Most findings were replicated in PRESTO (n=2719). In contrast, several of these differences were reversed in the community (FHS, n=3539;FDR-significant): prolonged QTc was more common in women, whereas LVH, dementia, heart failure, and higher BMI were more common in men. Conclusions: Sex differences among SCA cases were mostly reproducible in SCA cohorts, and distinct from sex-related patterns in the community. These results have implications for development of sex-specific SCA risk assessment and prevention strategies.

data.title: Preprint: Improvements in patient-reported outcomes after neuromuscular electrical stimulation therapy for snoring and mild sleep apnea
data.authors: Crawford, M. R.; Jones, A. L.; Parthasarathy, S.; Osborne, C.; Walia, H.; Ojile, J.; Malhotra, A.
data.abstract: Objectives: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) offers alternative options to patients with Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) unable to tolerate first line treatment. Randomized controlled trial data suggest efficacy of NMES treatment in improving OSA outcomes, snoring and sleepiness; however, no study to our knowledge has examined the effects on a range of daytime patient reported outcomes in a large real-world sample. Methods: This report presents clinical data from 472 patients completing NMES treatment. Bayesian linear mixed models were used to analyze pre-to-post treatment changes in mood (PHQ8), sleep disturbance (PROMIS-SD-4a), sleep related impairment (PROMIS-SRI-4a), and functioning (FOSQ), whilst controlling for key covariates. Posterior probabilities were calculated to estimate the probability of a change in symptoms (P(effect > 0)) and probability of exceeding a minimal clinically important difference (P(effect > MCID)). Results: The posterior probabilities of an improvement in scores in sleep disturbance (mean change -6.1, 94% HDI: -3.8 to -8.5) and sleep-related impairment (mean change -10.0, 94% HDI: -5.4 to -14), depression (mean change -3.5, 94% HDI: -1.7 to -5.2), at posttreatment were greatest and varied between 99.8 to 100%. Probability of change in functioning was low (60.9% chance of improvement). These effects remained when controlling for age, gender, treatment adherence, mean intensity and variance in intensity. Probabilities for MCI change for mood, sleep disturbance and sleep-related impairment were high (86-91%). Conclusions: The results from this report highlight the potential impact NMES therapy has on patient reported outcomes. These findings are in support of prior randomized placebo-controlled data and several observational cohort studies for NMES as treatment for mild OSA.

data.title: Preprint: Comprehensive real-world utilization, treatment trajectories, and outcomes of immune checkpoint inhibitors across cancer types: the multicenter FAIR-ICI cohort
data.authors: Ha, L. T.; Ver Donck, F.; Bassez, I.; Oeste, C. L.; Vulsteke, C.; Delombaerde, D.; Hens, D.; Prenen, H.; Croes, L.; De Meulenaere, A.; Debruyne, P. R.; Verhaert, M.; Aspeslagh, S.; Brusselaers, N.; Verbiest, A.
data.abstract: Background: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed cancer treatment, yet evidence on their utilization, treatment trajectories, and effectiveness in routine clinical practice remains limited. We characterized real-world ICI use and outcomes across cancer types using the multicenter FAIR-ICI cohort and explored differences between real-world and pivotal trial outcomes. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults receiving ICIs across four Belgian hospitals. Structured and unstructured electronic health record data were harmonized using the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model (OMOP-CDM) and natural language processing. We evaluated overall survival (OS), time on treatment (ToT), time to next treatment (TTNT), ICI discontinuation (>12-week treatment gap without re-initiation), and post-discontinuation survival. OS was descriptively compared with pivotal trials, and prognostic factors were assessed using multivariable Cox regression. An interactive public dashboard was developed to enable exploration of cohort characteristics, treatment patterns, and outcomes. Results: Among 3,231 ICI-treated patients, 2,514 (77.8%) had metastatic disease. Among metastatic patients, 568 (22.6%) discontinued ICI without subsequent systemic therapy. Median post-discontinuation OS was 21.4 months (95% CI 16.5-37.2), with 49.1% alive at 24 months. ToT and TTNT were generally shorter than OS, particularly in melanoma (median OS 78 months; ToT 7 months; TTNT 26 months). Real-world survival was frequently less favorable than in pivotal trials. ECOG >=2 was associated with poorer OS than ECOG 0-1 (adjusted HR 2.18, 95% CI 1.82-2.60). In NSCLC patients receiving pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy, survival with ECOG 0-1 more closely approximated trial outcomes, whereas survival with ECOG >=2 was substantially poorer. Conclusions: Real-world ICI treatment trajectories extend beyond active treatment, with some patients experiencing prolonged survival after discontinuation. Differences between real-world and trial outcomes highlight the importance of patient characteristics, particularly performance status, when interpreting trial evidence in routine care. FAIR-ICI provides a scalable framework for evaluating real-world immunotherapy effectiveness, treatment trajectories, and future investigations of treatment-related toxicity.

data.title: Preprint: Elevated Maternal Glycated Albumin is Associated with Large for Gestational Age Infants: Results from a Prospective Longitudinal Study
data.authors: Ferreira Jorgensen, C.; Chillon, T. S.; Scavenius, C.; Sacks, D. B.; Raghuraman, B.; Bekker-Nielsen, D.; Bache, N.; Vorm, O.; Rode, L.; Ekelund, C.; Damm, P.; Hojlund, K.; Jensen, D. M.; Clausen, T. D.; McIntyre, H. D.; Overgaard, M.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Clinical Biochemistry, Odense University Hospital, Odense, Denmark
data.abstract: Aims/hypothesis Glycated albumin (GA) has been shown to be a moderate predictor of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), while evidence supporting its role in predicting adverse pregnancy outcomes remains limited. Here, we aimed to perform a comparative study of GA and haemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) for predicting GDM and large-for-gestational-age (LGA) infants in a prospective cohort. Methods We developed a rapid liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry method for measuring site-specific albumin glycation. GA was quantified at two glycation sites, GA (KQT) and GA (KLV), as well as their sum, GA-total. GA was measured in stored serum samples collected at 11-14 and 23-31 gestational weeks from 465 participants in the single-centre observational cohort. HbA1c was measured routinely at each visit. Linear mixed-effects models were used to compare GA between participants with and without GDM (n=100) or LGA (n=57). Logistic regression was used to estimate odds ratios (ORs) for GDM and LGA according to GA and HbA1c. Results GA was lower in women who developed GDM during early pregnancy compared to non-GDM controls (GA-total; p=0.004), while in mid-late pregnancy, only GA (KQT) was lower in women with GDM (p=0.036). In contrast, HbA1c was higher in women with GDM at both timepoints compared to non-GDM controls (p<0.001) and higher HbA1c was associated with increased odds of GDM (OR=2.20, p<0.001; OR=2.30, p<0.001, respectively). GA was higher in the LGA group, in both early (GA-total; p=0.032) and mid-late pregnancy (GA-total; p=0.030) and associated with increased odds of LGA (GA-total; OR=1.59, p=0.009; GA-total; OR=1.46, p=0.019, respectively). HbA1c was not associated with LGA at either timepoint. Conclusions/interpretation Higher GA in early and mid-late pregnancy were associated with an increased risk of LGA, whereas no significant association was observed for HbA1c. GA may therefore provide risk assessment beyond HbA1c for identifying pregnancies at risk of fetal overgrowth.

data.title: Preprint: Cerebral white matter integrity in Type-2 Diabetes Mellitus and integrated role of Interleukin-6: Findings in multiethnic middle-aged and older US-adults
data.authors: Hallab, A.; The Health and Aging Brain Study (HABS-HD) Study Team,
data.abstract: Introduction: Peripheral neural injuries, known as polyneuropathy, are largely described in patients with Type-2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM). However, less is known about the T2DM-associated cerebral White Matter (WM) integrity. Previous studies highlighted mediating effects of inflammation in the T2DM-brain association. It is, however, still unclear whether Interleukin-6 (IL-6) mediates specifically T2DM-cerebral WM integrity. Methods: The multiethnic 50 years and older study population is a subset of the Health and Aging Brain Study: Health Disparities (HABS-HD) study. Diffusion-weighted scans were analyzed, and diffusion parameters were averaged in major WM tracts. Effect sizes (Cohen s d) were calculated after adjusting for relevant confounders. Mediation analysis was performed using 1000-fold non-parametric bootstrapping of 95% confidence intervals (CI). The results were adjusted for multiple testing using the False Discovery Rate method (FDR). Results: Several WM tracts showed significant impairment in T2DM participants after adjusting for confounders and multiple testing (posterior thalamic radiation (adj. Cohen s d=0.14[0.03-024]), anterior corona radiata (adj. Cohen s d=0.15[0.04-0.26]), cingulum (adj. Cohen s d=0.14[0.03-0.25]), inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (adj. Cohen s d=0.16[0.06-0.27]), genu of the corpus callosum (adj. Cohen s d=0.13[0.03-0.24]), and body of the corpus callosum (adj. Cohen s d=0.28[0.17-0.38])). Within two years, the effect sizes showed an increasing trend. Even in cognitively unimpaired participants, T2DM was associated with locally reduced WM integrity. IL-6 statistically mediated up to 15% of these major associations. Conclusions: The study demonstrated T2DM-associated impairment of intracerebral WM integrity. In T2DM, microstructural WM changes might start before clinically objectified cognitive impairment. The role of systemic inflammation needs to be assessed in causal frameworks.

data.title: Preprint: Target Trial Emulation of Metformin for Dementia Prevention in All of Us: Robustness to Cohort and Confounder Definitions
data.authors: Charpignon, M.-L.; Shnitzer, T.; Iraqui, A.; Pace, D. F.; Maddah, M.; Uhler, C.
data.abstract: Metformin use has been associated with a lower risk of incident dementia than other antidiabetics. We perform target trial emulation and causal competing risk analysis in the NIH All of Us (AoU) Research Program database, contrasting the effects of metformin and sulfonylurea initiation on dementia onset and death without dementia. AoU's social and behavioral health data allowed us to test robustness to excluding such confounders, and we further adjusted for calendar year effects and prior antidiabetic exposure, using both semiparametric Cox proportional hazards (PH) models and nonparametric models. Under stabilized inverse propensity score of treatment weighting, metformin was associated with a substantially lower risk of death (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.61, 95% CI: [0.49, 0.75]) and a lower incidence of dementia (HR: 0.90, 95% CI: [0.82, 1.02]). Estimated HRs were closely aligned with estimates obtained in the UK primary care and US Mass General Brigham health systems. This finding was robust to the inclusion of participants without a type 2 diabetes diagnosis at baseline and to the consideration of different covariate sets in the propensity score model, supporting metformin as a promising candidate for dementia prevention and motivating prospective validation.

data.title: Preprint: Association between trajectories of breastfeeding duration and infant health: Prospective cohort study
data.authors: Dessy, T.; Dennis, C.-L.
data.abstract: Background: Breastfeeding is a modifiable pathway contributing to infant health. Objectives: To estimate trajectories of breastfeeding and the association between trajectories of breastfeeding and infant health. Methods: We conducted a prospective longitudinal cohort study (2014-2020, Canada) with 3217 cohabitating English-literate mother-father-infant triads with internet or telephone access. data.title: Preprint: Maternal ADHD and exclusive breastfeeding: A prospective community-based cohort study
data.authors: Dessy, T.; Dennis, C.-L.
data.abstract: Importance: Maternal attention-deficit disorder with or without hyperactivity (ADHD) is an established risk factor for adverse perinatal outcomes that remains understudied to breastfeeding. Objective: To estimate the effect of maternal ADHD on 6-month exclusive breastfeeding. Design: A prospective longitudinal community-based cohort study. Setting: Canada, 2014-2020. Participants: We included 3217 English-literate mother-father dyads with internet or telephone access, comprising women with singleton birth within 3 weeks postpartum (study baseline) and were cohabiting with the biological father. Women with major psychiatric conditions or suicidality were excluded. All participants provided informed consent at recruitment. Data were collected online through self-report questionnaires. Exposure: Maternal ADHD was measured at baseline using the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (sum of scores [≥]14). Main Outcomes and Measures: We defined 6-month exclusive breastfeeding based on maternal reported infant feeding, assessed at 3 and 6 months. Maternal childhood adversity (Adverse Childhood Experiences International Questionnaire, ACE-IQ; sum score) was included as a confounder. The average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) was estimated using linear probability models. We calculated 95% percentile bootstrap CI. Missing data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations with 10 iterations. Results: Complete-case analyses included 2071/3217 mother-father dyads, most of which were Canadian-born (79%). Childhood adversity, mental health conditions, and substance use were higher among mothers who screened positive for ADHD (4%) than among those who did not: the median number of ACE was 5 IQR 4-6; 38% self-reported prenatal depression, 13% smoked cigarettes and 19% drank alcohol during pregnancy; 11% of infants used the neonatal intensive care unit. Notably, though 90% of mothers with ADHD intended to breastfeed exclusively only 28% breastfed exclusively for 6 months. Among families with maternal ADHD, the effect of maternal ADHD on 6-month exclusive breastfeeding was ATT -0.105, 95% CI -0.209 to -0.003 in the model adjusted for maternal ACE and paternal ADHD. With multiple imputation: ATT -0.109, 95% CI -0.213 to -0.004. Conclusions and Relevance: Mothers with ADHD intend to breastfeed their infants exclusively, but additional challenges shorten the duration of exclusive breastfeeding, indicating a need for interventions tailored to neurodevelopmental differences.

data.title: Preprint: Polydrug use and recreational motives are associated with lower posttraumatic symptoms in survivors of a mass trauma event
data.authors: Magal, N.; Netzer, O.; Epstein, D. H.; Shaham, Y.; Repantis, D.; Lev-Ran, S.; Harduf, A.; Admon, R.; Salomon, R.
data.author_corresponding_institution: School of Psychological Sciences, University of Haifa, Haifa, Israel; Integrated Brain and Behavior Research Center (IBBRC), University of Haifa, Haifa, Israel;
data.abstract: Objective: Drug use after trauma is common, but polydrug use patterns, motives, and associations with subsequent symptoms are poorly understood. We examined these associations among mass-casualty terror attack survivors, 72% of whom used drugs immediately before trauma exposure. Methods: Survivors of the October 7, 2023 Nova Festival attack reported use of six drug types (alcohol, cannabis, ketamine, stimulants, MDMA, psychedelics) and motives (avoidance, emotional regulation, self-medication, sleep, recreation) longitudinally at three timepoints (TP): 1-6 months (N=772), 8-12 months (N=453), and 17-24 months (N=302) post-attack. Separate latent class analyses of TP2 data characterized drug use, motives, and their combination. Linear regression and mixed-effects models examined associations between class membership and PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) scores, adjusting for age, sex, time since trauma, and TP1 PCL-5 scores. Results: At TP2, 70% reported polydrug use, 17% used one drug, and 13% reported no use. The high drug-load class (mean 4.6 drug types) had lower PCL-5 scores than the low drug-load class (mean 1.5 drug types); this difference was evident among participants using [≥]4 drug types and persisted through TP3. The self-medication-motive class had higher PCL-5 scores than the recreational-motive class. In joint analyses, recreational-motive users at both low and high drug loads had lower PCL-5 scores than participants reporting self-medication motives and primarily cannabis use. Conclusions: Polydrug use was common among the mass-trauma survivors in our study. Self-medication motives were associated with higher PTSD symptom severity than recreational motives. Unexpectedly, higher polydrug use was associated with lower PTSD symptom scores.

data.title: Preprint: ACCURACY OF COMPRESSED SENSING ACCELERATED 3D-FLAIR IN THE DIAGNOSTIC WORK-UP OF MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS AT 1.5 T
data.authors: Iacoban, C. G.; Klüner, C.; Bösenberg, H.; Alykova, O.; Gerdes, M.; Reuter, S.; Mathys, C.; Sundermann, B.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Radiology and Neuroradiology, Evangelisches Krankenhaus Oldenburg, Steinweg 13-17, 26122 Oldenburg, Niedersachsen, Germany
data.abstract: BACKGROUND: 3D-FLAIR is central to MR-based diagnosis and monitoring of MS, but long acquisition times remain a limitation. OBJECTIVES: This single-center prospective non-inferiority study evaluated whether compressed sensing (CS) - accelerated 3D-FLAIR at 1.5T provides lesion detection comparable to optimized Generalized Autocalibrating Partially Parallel Acquisition (GRAPPA) - accelerated 3D-FLAIR. Optimized CS- and GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-FLAIR sequences were incorporated into MRI examinations in patients with known or suspected MS. The primary endpoint was manual lesion count by two blinded readers using a 10% non-inferiority margin. Secondary endpoints included image quality, SNR, CNR, and automated lesion count and volumetry. RESULTS: Sixty-eight patients were included (mean age, 40.1+/-13.3 years; 61.8% women). CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR reduced acquisition time by 31.8% compared with GRAPPA (4:00 vs 5:52 minutes). Non-inferiority for manual lesion count was demonstrated for both readers (reader A, p < .0001; reader B, p = .005). Interrater agreement was excellent for CS (ICC = 0.921; 95% CI, 0.837-0.957) and very good for GRAPPA (ICC = 0.851; 95% CI, 0.769-0.906). Subjective image quality was high for both techniques. GRAPPA showed higher objective signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise-ratio (CNR), whereas automated lesion counts and volumes were higher for CS. CONCLUSION: CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR provided non-inferior lesion detection with substantial scan-time reduction.

data.title: Preprint: PROSPECTIVE COMPARISON OF OPTIMIZED COMPRESSED SENSING AND GRAPPA-ACCELERATED 3D-TOF-MRA FOR EVALUATION OF UNTREATED INTRACRANIAL ANEURYSMS AT 1.5 T: A NON-INFERIORITY STUDY
data.authors: Iacoban, C. G.; Bösenberg, H.; Klüner, C.; Alykova, O.; Gerdes, M.; Meinert, F.; Sundermann, B.; Mathys, C.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Radiology and Neuroradiology, Evangelisches Krankenhaus Oldenburg, Steinweg 13-17, 26122 Oldenburg, Niedersachsen, Germany
data.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES 3D-TOF-MRA is a standard non-invasive method for detecting and monitoring intracranial aneurysms, but long scan times remain a limitation. Compressed sensing (CS) acceleration for intracranial aneurysm evaluation has mainly been studied at 3T. This prospective single-center non-inferiority study compared CS-accelerated 3D-TOF at 1.5T with GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-TOF-MRA for evaluating untreated intracranial aneurysms. MATERIALS AND METHODS Sample size was determined via a preliminary retrospective study. 25 patients with 32 untreated aneurysms underwent both CS- (factor 7, 3:04 min) and GRAPPA-accelerated (factor 2, 5:00 min) 3D-TOF, yielding a 38.7% scan-time reduction. Two blinded neuroradiologists assessed overall image quality (primary endpoint) and artifacts, subjective CNR, aneurysm delineation and diameters (secondary endpoints). Non-inferiority was tested via one-sided t-test (prespecified 10% margin); interrater agreement used ICC. RESULTS CS demonstrated non-inferiority to GRAPPA for overall image quality in both readers (p <= .023), though interrater agreement was low (ICC 0.241-0.262), reflecting subjective variability. Secondary exploratory analyses showed heterogeneous preferences. ROI-based CNR was lower for CS (median 169.6; IQR, 91.0-226. vs. 278.2; 181.0-366.2). Aneurysm diameter measurements showed excellent interrater agreement for both techniques (CS ICC, 0.899-0.980; GRAPPA ICC, 0.877-0.973; all p < .001). CONCLUSION CS-accelerated 3D-TOF at 1.5T met non-inferiority criteria vs. GRAPPA-TOF for overall image quality, reducing scan time by 38.7% while preserving aneurysm measurement reliability. However, reduced CNR and reader-preference variability important trade-offs.

data.title: Preprint: Fibromuscular Dysplasia in Acute Type A Aortic Dissection: A Common yet Underrecognized Vascular Phenotype in Women
data.authors: Weustink, A. C.; Keijzer, A. R.; Budde, R. P. J.; Versmissen, J.; Galema, T. W.; Veen, K. M.; Takkenberg, J. J. M.; Arabkhani, B.; Coenen, A.
data.abstract: Objectives: Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) is a non inflammatory, non atherosclerotic arterial disease characterized by multifocal arterial beading that predominantly affects women. Although FMD commonly involves the renal and carotid arteries, its relationship with acute type A aortic dissection (ATAAD) remains poorly understood. We investigated the proportion of patients with FMD among patients with ATAAD, focusing on sex based differences. Materials and Methods: Patients aged below 70 years with ATAAD and ECG triggered aortic CT angiography (CTA) were consecutively included in this retrospective single-center study. FMD was defined as multifocal arterial beading (string-of-beads appearance) in at least one vascular territory, according to international consensus criteria. The highest-quality CTA examination was evaluated by an experienced cardiovascular radiologist. All suspected FMD cases were independently reviewed by a second experienced cardiovascular radiologist, with the final diagnosis established by consensus. Proportions were reported with 95% confidence intervals and compared between sexes . Results: Of 214 patients screened, 200 were included (138 men and 62 women). FMD was confirmed in 18/200 patients (9%; 95% CI, 6 till 14%), none of whom had a prior FMD diagnosis. FMD was more frequent in women (12/62, 19%; 95% CI, 11 till 31%) than men (6/138, 4%; 95% CI, 2 till 9%; P<0.001). FMD predominantly involved the renal arteries. Additional carotid CTA was available in 49/200 patients (25%) and in 7/18 patients with FMD (39%); three of these seven patients had carotid FMD. Conclusion: FMD was observed in a substantial proportion of patients presenting with ATAAD, particularly women. These findings suggest that FMD is an underrecognized vascular phenotype in patients with ATAAD.

data.title: Preprint: Screening for rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease using lung ultrasound: a systematic review and quality appraisal of recent studies
data.authors: Copoeru, A. D.; Mocan, M.; Farcas, A.; Vlaicu, S.; Chira, R. I.
data.author_corresponding_institution: "Iuliu Hatieganu" University of Medicine and Pharmacy
data.abstract: Interstitial lung diseases (ILD) associated with systemic autoimmune disease can have a strong negative impact on patient outcomes. The diagnostic gold standard is high-resolution computer tomography (HRCT). Numerous studies have proven lung ultrasound's (LUS) utility in ILD, as well as other lung pathologies. Recently, there has been more focus on ILD in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), a previously overlooked complication, and screening methods. The purpose of this systematic review was to summarize the recent knowledge regarding LUS compared to HRCT in screening ILD in RA patients. We reviewed relevant literature from the last 10 years and selected 10 articles. Results show that LUS is effective compared to HRCT as a screening tool. Several diagnostic and severity scores have been elaborated and tested. Further focus should be on LUS in long-term follow-up and standardization of protocols.

data.title: Preprint: Enhancing deep sleep with auditory stimulation to boost cognitive training responsiveness in people with Parkinson's disease and mild cognitive impairment: Rationale and design of the double-blind randomized controlled trial PD-CogT-Sleep
data.authors: Ophey, A.; Kleinsorge, M. T.; Wallimann, N. A.; Maric, A.; Loosli, S. V.; Mollenhauer, B.; Balint, B.; Huber, R.; Baumann, C. R.; Kalbe, E.; Schreiner, S. J.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurology, University Hospital Zurich, University of Zurich, 8091 Zurich, Switzerland; Clinical Neuroscience Center, University Hospital Zurich, U
data.abstract: Background: Cognitive training (CogT) is an established non-pharmacological intervention for people with Parkinson's disease (PD) and mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI). However, overall effects on cognitive outcomes are small to moderate and interindividually highly heterogeneous. Sleep -especially deep sleep- could be an important determinant of CogT responsiveness in PD, and may have beneficial effects on PD pathophysiology. Therefore, the enhancement of deep sleep by phase-targeted auditory stimulation (PTAS) could strengthen the effects of CogT on cognitive symptoms and counteract disease progression. Methods: PD-CogT-Sleep is a monocentric, partly decentralized, double-blind, randomized sham-controlled trial that combines two remotely delivered non-pharmacological interventions, to assess the additive effect of PTAS on digital CogT responsiveness in people with PD-MCI. The primary outcome is executive functions; Secondary and exploratory outcomes include further cognitive functions, participant-reported outcome measures, blood-based biomarkers, and high-density sleep electroencephalography markers. Outcomes are assessed at baseline, five weeks post-allocation and at 3-month follow-up. We aim to consecutively recruit N=50 participants, who will be randomized 1:1 to receive CogT+PTAS or CogT+Sham. Discussion: The PD-CogT-Sleep study integrates wearable and digital technologies to systematically combine a novel, non-invasive, sleep-enhancing intervention (PTAS) with established CogT to improve cognition and evaluate PTAS' disease-modifying potential through its effects on blood-based biomarkers in PD-MCI. The expected results will foster our understanding of the interplay of sleep, cognition, and neurodegeneration, and may guide further development of safe, feasible, scalable, patient-centered, technology-based non-pharmacological interventions counteracting cognitive decline in neurodegenerative diseases.

D.; Von Allmen, G.; Schust Myers, L.; Egan, S.; Babineaux, B.; Simms, S.; Craig, K.; Manaster, L.; Johnson, S.; Fox, P.; Sills, J.; Rushing, G.; Scheffer, I. E.; Thakur, N.; Lal, D.
data.abstract: Background and Objectives: Motor dysfunction is a major contributor to disability in pediatric-onset monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), yet systematic quantifications of motor phenotypes across development using validated clinical scales remain underdeveloped. Existing studies have classified motor phenotypes rather than quantified domain-specific severity, limiting their use as outcome measures in clinical trials. Here, we systematically quantify motor dysfunction using established clinical rating scales to explore their utility as motor endpoints. Methods: In this cross-sectional observational study, 102 individuals with NDDs (0.5-38 years) secondary to pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in five genes (SCN2A, KCNQ2, CSNK2A1, CACNA1A, SCN8A) and 31 unaffected sibling controls underwent standardized motor assessments using the Scale for Assessment and Rating of Ataxia, Burke-Fahn-Marsden Dystonia Scale, and the Modified Ashworth Scale. Regional and functional categorization of parameters enabled differentiated interpretation. Gene-specific patterns were evaluated using z-score standardization across the pooled affected cohort, with gene-level averaging and nonparametric bootstrap-derived 95% confidence intervals. Results: Dysfunction was present in individuals with NDDs across speech (90%), coordination (87%), dystonia (83.3%), gross motor (82.4%) and spasticity (42.2%), with minimal impairment in controls (0-12.9%). We observed substantial heterogeneity across motor domains and subdomains; ataxic dysarthria had the highest score distribution (median 0.83 [IQR, 0.17-1.0]), whereas spasticity showed near-floor scores. Individuals with SCN2A variants demonstrated higher mean z-scores across multiple subdomains than other genes, with more consistent deviations observed in coordination and speech domains (Coordination: mean z = 0.29, 95% CI 0.03-0.54; Speech: mean z = 0.3, 95% CI 0.03-0.57), whereas domain-specific or less pronounced patterns were observed in other genes. The ataxia and dystonia scales demonstrated low floor and ceiling effects. Discussion: Using three clinical scales across a broad developmental and functional range, our study moves motor phenotyping in monogenic NDDs from categorical description toward quantitative, domain-resolved severity assessment. Exploratory analysis indicates marked heterogeneity in severity profiles across genes, most notably in SCN2A, suggesting potential selective motor vulnerability. These findings provide evidence for the feasibility of motor phenotyping and provide preliminary, cross-sectional benchmark severity distributions. Subsequent longitudinal validation and validation in larger, longitudinal, and variant-stratified cohorts will enable natural history studies and future therapeutic trials alongside seizure outcomes.

data.title: Preprint: Variant Classification of a Non-Protein Coding Gene: ACMG/AMP Specifications for RMRP from the Clinical Genome Resource Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Disease Variant Curation Expert Panel
data.authors: Jacovas, V. C.; Demirkol, Y.; Nieto-Patlan, A.; Martin, S.; McNulty, S.; Allenspach, E. J.; Vakkilainen, S.; Notarangelo, L. D.; Puck, J. M.; Walter, J.; Chan, A. Y.; Cowan, M. J.; Hershfield, M. S.; van Oers, N. S. C.; Verbsky, J.; Chung, B. H.-Y.; Ghosh, R.; Luo, X.; Piazza, M.; Schulze, K. V.; Sivakumaran, T. A.; Yuan, B.; Johnson, B. A.; Chinn, I. K.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Pediatrics, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, TX; Division of Pediatric Immunology, Allergy, and Retrovirology, Texas Childrens Hospital, Houst
data.abstract: Purpose: This study, conducted by the Clinical Genome Resource Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Disease Variant Curation Expert Panel (ClinGen SCID-VCEP), aimed to adapt the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics/Association for Molecular Pathology (ACMG/AMP) framework for germline variant interpretation in RMRP. Unlike the protein-coding genes for which the framework was primarily developed, RMRP encodes a non-protein-coding RNA. Biallelic pathogenic variants in RMRP cause cartilage-hair hypoplasia, which can include severe combined immunodeficiency disease and other immune abnormalities. Methods: An RMRP-focused SCID-VCEP subgroup reviewed all 28 ACMG/AMP evidence criteria using population databases, published clinical and experimental data, computational predictions, and expert consensus. Each criterion was retained, modified, or designated as not applicable based on RMRP biology and disease mechanisms. The resulting specifications were pilot tested using 27 variants selected from ClinVar and research laboratory data. Results: Fifteen ACMG/AMP criteria were determined to be applicable to RMRP, while 13 were considered not applicable. Several criteria were modified to evaluate nucleotide-level effects on transcriptional regulation, critical promoter regions, and RNA secondary structure. The specifications also incorporated RMRP-specific recommendations for population frequency, functional evidence, variant phase, segregation, and phenotype. Application of the specifications classified 6 variants as pathogenic, 10 as likely pathogenic, 7 as variants of uncertain significance, and 4 as benign. Previously pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants remained within the pathogenic spectrum, and all previously benign variants remained benign. Variants with conflicting ClinVar interpretations were resolved as either likely pathogenic or uncertain. PM1, PM3, and PP4 were the primary criteria supporting pathogenic classifications. Conclusion: The SCID-VCEP specifications provide a standardized approach to the classification of germline RMRP variants in cartilage-hair hypoplasia and demonstrate how the ACMG/AMP framework can be adapted for a disease-associated non-protein-coding RNA gene. These specifications support the development of variant interpretation frameworks for other clinically relevant non-protein-coding genes.

data.title: Preprint: Effects of Pantoprazole Based on Dialysis Status: A Protocol and Statistical Analysis Plan for a Secondary Analysis of the REVISE Trial
data.authors: Thabane, A.; Rewa, O.; Heels-Ansdell, D.; Bagshaw, S. M.; Jeong, R.; Borthwick, M.; Adhikari, N. K.; Zampieri, F. G.; Ostermann, M.; Muscedere, J.; Marshall, J.; Deane, A.; Lauzier, F.; Arabi, Y. M.; Kuriyama, A.; Burns, K.; Yarnell, C. J.; Vazquez Grande, G.; Zytaruk, N.; Cook, D. J.; REVISE Investigators,  ; Canadian Critical Care Trials Group,  ; Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Clinical Trials Group,
data.category: intensive care and critical care medicine
data.abstract: Background A recent international randomized trial found that the proton pump inhibitor (PPI) pantoprazole significantly reduced the risk of clinically important upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding among invasively ventilated patients in the intensive care unit (ICU), with no effect on mortality. Pantoprazole may be of particularly high utility among patients at high-risk of bleeding, such as those receiving renal replacement therapy (RRT) prior to ICU admission. However, given the complex mechanisms by which renal insufficiency may increase bleeding risk, as well as the possible association between PPI use and adverse kidney outcomes, investigating whether kidney failure treated with RRT at baseline modifies the treatment effect of PPIs is clinically relevant. Methods We have planned a post hoc secondary analysis of the Re-evaluating the Inhibition of Stress Erosions (REVISE) Trial (NCT03374800). The primary objective if this study is to evaluate whether any RRT on study day 1 (e.g., maintenance RRT in the outpatient setting, or RRT initiated in the hospital [intermittent hemodialysis, continuous renal replacement therapy, sustained low efficiency dialysis, or peritoneal dialysis]) modifies the treatment effect of pantoprazole on clinically important upper GI bleeding and 90-day mortality. The secondary objective is to evaluate whether maintenance RRT (intermittent hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis) in an outpatient setting before the index hospital admission modifies the effect of pantoprazole on clinically important upper GI bleeding and 90-day mortality. Secondary outcomes for both analyses are patient important upper GI bleeding, ICU and hospital mortality. We will perform Cox proportional-hazard analyses, including the RRT exposure of interest, randomized group, and their interaction for each outcome, reporting results as hazards ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and p-values for the interaction term. Conclusion Results of this study will inform critical care practice, particularly for the care of patients at risk of stress-related GI ulceration in the ICU who have received RRT.

data.title: Preprint: Oral rehydration salts and zinc for childhood diarrhoea in Bangladesh, 2019 and 2025: coverage, wealth inequality and reported source of care
data.authors: Hoque, S. M. A. U.; Hasan, M. K.; Rahman, M. A.; Islam, M. K.; Ahmed, T.; Haque, S. M. R.; Islam, M. R.; Baset, K. u.
data.abstract: Background: Diarrhoea remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality among children under five. WHO and UNICEF recommend oral rehydration salts (ORS) alongside 10 to 14 days of zinc supplementation. However, national progress in combined treatment coverage and its socioeconomic and care-related inequalities remains insufficiently understood in Bangladesh. We assessed combined coverage, wealth inequality and differences by reported source of care. Methods: We analysed children under five with caregiver-reported diarrhoea in the 2019 (n=1,589) and 2025 (n=1,634) Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS). We estimated combined coverage using design-based methods, wealth inequality using slope indices, and associations with source of care using pooled adjusted prevalence ratios (aPR). Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) estimates provided an external comparison. Results: Combined ORS and zinc coverage increased from 35.0% (95% CI 32.3 to 37.7) in 2019 to 42.9% (40.1 to 45.8) in 2025. In 2025, ORS and zinc coverage were 75.8% and 51.9%, respectively. The 2025 estimate agreed with DHS 2022, whereas MICS 2019 was below DHS 2017-18. Wealth inequality persisted in 2025 (slope index 13.0 percentage points, 3.4 to 22.6). Adjustment attenuated the pooled slope index from 11.8 to 6.5 points (-1.7 to 14.6). Coverage was lower with pharmacy-only than public care (aPR 0.59, 0.53 to 0.66) and with no care reported (0.14, 0.11 to 0.18). Children with no care reported accounted for 43.7% of children without combined treatment in 2025. Conclusions: Combined coverage increased, although the apparent progress may be overstated by the lower MICS 2019 estimate relative to DHS. Zinc remained the larger treatment gap, while one in four children received no ORS. Reported sources of care require cautious interpretation.

data.title: Preprint: The impact of warning labels versus traffic light labels on food choice and negative emotional responses: two randomised controlled trials among UK adult populations with and without an eating disorder
data.authors: Evans, R. K.; Latham, R.; Finlay, A.; Robinson, E.
data.abstract: Background In the UK, front-of-pack traffic light labels (TLL) are implemented voluntarily. The UK Government are considering alternative FOP approaches, such as nutrient warning labels (WL). However, the effects and potential harm of TLL versus WL in UK consumers are unclear. We compared the effects of WL, TLL, and no label on unhealthy food item selection and negative affect among UK adults with and without an eating disorder (ED). Methods We conducted two online randomised controlled trials. In Study 1, 924 UK adults without an ED diagnosis were randomly assigned (1:1:1) to a WL, TLL, or no labels condition and completed a food-choice task. In Study 2, 240 UK adults with an ED diagnosis completed a baseline no-label food choice task and were subsequently randomly assigned (1:1:1) to WL, TLL, or no labels for a follow-up food choice task. The primary outcome was the number of task-specific unhealthy food items selected. Negative affect before and after food choice tasks was measured as a secondary outcome. Findings In Study 1 (data collected 02/25 - 04/25), unhealthy food selection differed by condition (p = .013). Of five products selected, WL participants selected 0.20 fewer unhealthy items than TLL participants (8.0%; p = .038) and 0.28 fewer than controls (10.7%; p = .004). In Study 2 (data collected 11/25 - 02/26), unhealthy selection decreased by 0.39 items with WL (17.7%; p = .015), 0.13 with TLL (5.3%, p = .286), and 0.00 with no labels. The reduction was greater with WL than with no labels (p = .029). Label condition did not differentially affect task-related negative affect in either study (Study 1, p = .757; Study 2, p = .448). Interpretation WL tended to be associated with lower unhealthy food selection compared to TLL in UK adults. There was minimal evidence that WL or TLL caused negative emotional responses. Funding This research was funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Oxford Health BRC. The views expressed are those of the author(s) and not necessarily those of the NIHR or the Department of Health and Social Care. Registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07339969

data.title: Preprint: Diagnostic Feature Associations in Atypical Parkinsonian Disorders: A Survey of Movement Disorders Specialists
data.authors: Zweber, C.; Iyer, V.; Houston, E.; Boyd, J. T.; Golbe, L.; Bruno, M. K.; Gupta, D. K.
data.author_corresponding_institution: John A. Burns School of Medicine, University of Hawaii
data.abstract: Objective: For the atypical parkinsonian disorders (APDs), including dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), multiple system atrophy (MSA), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), and corticobasal degeneration (CBD), accurate antemortem diagnosis remains clinically challenging because of overlapping features, phenotypic heterogeneity, and limited definitive biomarkers. Consensus diagnostic criteria are complex and may not reflect how clinicians operationalize diagnostic reasoning in practice. Methods: We surveyed movement disorders specialists regarding diagnostic implications of 32 clinical features, comparing the results with a 2024 consensus algorithmic framework called the "General Neurologist's Practical Diagnostic Algorithm for APDs". We evaluated inter-rater agreement, diagnosis-level framework coverage, feature-level attribution patterns, and exact-set agreement. Results: Respondents demonstrated strong inter-specialist consensus in feature attribution (raw agreement 81.9%; Gwet's AC1 0.67, 95% CI 0.64-0.70). Specialist endorsement increased markedly with framework association strength, from 12.9% to 36.2% to 82.6% for unmapped, modest, and moderate associations respectively. Diagnosis-level coverage was higher for MSA, PSP, and CBD than for DLB. Exact-set agreement was substantially more variable and depended on whether modest associations were incorporated into the framework definition. Despite high self-reported familiarity with and use of published diagnostic criteria, respondents overwhelmingly expressed interest in a unified diagnostic framework for APDs with automated clinical decision support (CDS). Conclusions: Movement disorders specialists showed internally consistent feature-attribution patterns for archetypal features, while differing in the weighting and breadth assigned to weaker or overlapping associations. These findings are evidence for a gap between consensus schemas and specialist diagnostic reasoning and may inform future diagnostic frameworks and CDS approaches for the APDs.

data.title: Preprint: Assessment of Dissemination in Time in Multiple Sclerosis Using a Single 3D T2-FLAIR magnetic resonance imaging Radiomic Signature
data.authors: GUZMAN, E. G.; Casajuana-Larque, A.; Alberich, M.; Bollo, L.; Mongay-Ochoa, N.; Martinez-Heras, E.; Vidal-Jordana, A.; Montalban, X.; Tintore, M.; Rovira, A.; Sastre-Garriga, J.; Pareto, D.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Section of Neuroradiology Department of Radiology (IDI) Vall d'Hebron University Hospital
data.abstract: Background: In multiple sclerosis (MS), dissemination in time (DIT) is an important component of demonstrating disease activity and establishing the chronology of lesion development. DIT is routinely assessed from contrast-enhanced or follow-up magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Although proved useful, these methods are not without caveats motivating alternative approaches to study lesion chronology. We investigated whether single T2-FLAIR MRI contains sufficient information to distinguish temporally distinct MS lesion categories using radiomic features. Methods: In a retrospective longitudinal cohort of 273 participants with MS (1,311 MRI acquisitions), persistent brain lesions were temporally stratified using serial T2-FLAIR MRI. Long-standing established (LS-E) lesions were defined as observed for six years at least, and recent incident (R-I), as lesions that appeared over the span of two years in a follow-up MRI and were present until the last scan available. Radiomic features were extracted from lesion-level T2-FLAIR MRI. Feature selection was performed in an independent discovery cohort (Group 1, N=55). Selected features were then used to train a support vector machine classifier in a separate development cohort with repeated group-wise cross-validation (Group 2, N=163). Final performance was assessed in an held-out test cohort (Group 3, N=55). An exploratory analysis was then performed on baseline MRI from 64 subjects with clinically isolated syndrome (CIS), acquired after their first clinical demyelinating event. Results: Longitudinal tracking identified 814 classifiable lesions in Group 1, 3203 in Group 2, and 984 in Group 3. In Group 1, 18 radiomic features met predefined selection criteria (FDR-adjusted p smaller than 0.05 and absolute Cohen's d greater than 0.8), spanning intensity, shape, and texture domains. In the independent test cohort, the support vector machine classifier achieved an area under the curve of 0.78, with correct classification rates of 66% for R-I lesions and 73% for LS-E lesions. In the exploratory CIS analysis, predicted lesion temporal composition showed substantial inter-patient heterogeneity, with approximately one in ten participants presenting radiomic features compatible with LS-E lesions at their first clinical event. Conclusions: Single T2-FLAIR MRI contains measurable information related to MS lesion chronology. This proof-of-concept framework supports the feasibility of a line of research based on radiomics temporal lesion characterisation without contrast administration or dense longitudinal follow-up MRI, with potential relevance for studying lesion evolution and supporting DIT assessment.

In the independent test cohort, the support vector machine classifier achieved an area under the curve of 0.78, with correct classification rates of 66% for R-I lesions and 73% for LS-E lesions. In the exploratory CIS analysis, predicted lesion temporal composition showed substantial inter-patient heterogeneity, with approximately one in ten participants presenting radiomic features compatible with LS-E lesions at their first clinical event. Conclusions: Single T2-FLAIR MRI contains measurable information related to MS lesion chronology. This proof-of-concept framework supports the feasibility of a line of research based on radiomics temporal lesion characterisation without contrast administration or dense longitudinal follow-up MRI, with potential relevance for studying lesion evolution and supporting DIT assessment.

data.title: Preprint: Heterogeneous association between maternal haemoglobin concentration and child haemoglobin levels: a quantile regression analysis using multi-country nationally representative data.
data.authors: Amugsi, D. A.; Osuka, D.; Mwangi, B.; Jomo, S.; Ekiru, S.; Achaliwie, F.; Wilunda, C.
data.author_corresponding_institution: African Population and Health Research Center
data.abstract: Background: Low haemoglobin concentration, or anaemia, is a major global public health issue, particularly severe in sub-Saharan Africa, including East Africa, where prevalence rates are alarmingly high. This situation requires a comprehensive analysis to identify the key factors contributing to this high prevalence, especially in East Africa. This study uses robust quantile regression to examine the relationship between maternal haemoglobin concentration and child haemoglobin levels in three East African countries. Methods: The study analysed data from the Demographic and Health Surveys of three East African countries: Ethiopia, Tanzania, and Uganda. These data are nationally representative and are collected every five years from low- and middle-income countries. The analysis included a total sample of 6883 children and their mothers. The primary outcome variable was the haemoglobin concentration of the child. We used quantile regression to model the effects of maternal haemoglobin concentration on child haemoglobin levels, adjusting for potential confounders. Results: A one-unit increase in maternal haemoglobin concentration was associated with a unit increase in child haemoglobin concentration as follows: In Tanzania, the increases were 0.19, 0.20, 0.19, and 0.17 at the 5th, 10th, 25th, and 50th quantiles, respectively. In Ethiopia, the increases were 0.23, 0.22, 0.22, and 0.17 at the same quantiles. In Uganda, the increases were 0.19, 0.19, 0.18, and 0.19 at these quantiles. In contrast, a one-unit increase in maternal Hb concentration was associated with a smaller increase in child haemoglobin concentration, ranging from 0.11 to 0.13 at the 75th and 90th quantiles across all three countries. Overall, the most significant effects of maternal Hb concentration on child Hb levels were observed at the lower end of the conditional Hb distribution in each of the three countries. Conclusion: Maternal haemoglobin concentration is positively associated with children's haemoglobin levels across all countries studied. The strongest association is among children in the lower quantiles, who are at higher risk of anaemia. In contrast, the association is less pronounced among those in the upper quantiles. Therefore, improving maternal haemoglobin is likely to benefit children in the lower quantiles more than those in the upper quantiles. Programmes aimed at addressing child anaemia should consider these differing effects of maternal haemoglobin concentration. Keywords: Haemoglobin concentration, anaemia, maternal, child, quantile regression

data.title: Preprint: Analytical Validation and Clinical Implementation of MedGenome HRD Assay: A Large Comparative Study Against Commercial HRD Assays in Ovarian Cancer
data.authors: Rehman, S. M.; Shetty, R.; Magdalene, C. M.; Panda, M.; Ganesh, J. S.; Gupta, R.; Murugan, S.; L. Ramprasad, V.; N Dhabar, B.; Patil, S.; Kapoor, A.; Aggarwal, S.; Patil, T.; Pai, A.; Prasad, K.; Mishra, S. K.; Sathyanarayanan, V.; Pramanik, R.; Gupta, A.; Sansar, B.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Molecular Oncopathology, MedGenome Labs Limited., Bangalore, Karnataka, India
data.abstract: Background: Homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) is an important predictive biomarker for poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor (PARPi) therapy in ovarian cancer (OC). However, real-world data on HRD prevalence and assay performance in Indian patients are limited. This study evaluated commercial HRD assays, then developed an in-house HRD assay and characterized HRD and BRCA alterations in a large real-world Indian OC cohort. Methods: This retrospective study included 4,163 formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) OC samples tested between 2021 and 2025. HRD and BRCA status were initially assessed using the AmoyDx HRD Focus Panel (n=1,097) and SOPHiA DDM HRD Solution (n=470). Subsequently, 170 representative samples were used for the development and validation of an in-house HRD assay (MG_HRD), with external concordance assessed using the Myriad myChoice CDx assay in a subset of samples. Following validation, MG_HRD was implemented in routine clinical practice and applied to an independent cohort of 2,596 OC samples. HRD prevalence, BRCA mutation status, and clinicopathological associations were evaluated in all cohorts. Results: Among 4,163 ovarian cancer samples, HRD positivity was observed in 52.4% of cases, and pathogenic/likely pathogenic BRCA1/2 variants were identified in 23.6% of cases. Notably, 28.8% of tumors were BRCA wild-type but HRD-positive. BRCA-mutated tumors demonstrated significantly higher HRD genomic instability scores than BRCA wild-type tumors (p<0.001). HRD positivity was significantly enriched in high grade serous ovarian carcinomas. Remarkably, the BRCA1 c.68_69del (p.Glu23ValfsTer17) founder mutation was detected in 14.2% (97/685) of cases among the pathogenic variants in our study. The MG_HRD assay showed excellent concordance with commercial assays, achieving 97.1% overall agreement, 98.3% negative percent agreement (NPA), and 96.4% positive percent agreement (PPA), with complete concordance observed in the externally evaluated Myriad subset. Conclusions: This is the first Indian study to develop, validate, and implement an in-house HRD assay and evaluate HRD across three testing platforms in a large real-world OC cohort. The high prevalence of BRCA wild-type/HRD-positive tumors highlight the importance of comprehensive HRD testing, whereas the strong performance of MG_HRD supports its use as a reliable and cost-effective alternative for routine clinical practice. Keywords: ovarian cancer; homologous recombination deficiency; genomic instability, BRCA1/2, mutation, high grade serous carcinoma

data.title: Preprint: Unravelling the mechanisms of clozapine-induced neutropenia in treatment-resistant schizophrenia using cellular genomics
data.authors: Yang, Y.; Edwards, T.; Parat, M.-O.; Junker, N.; Neupane, S.; Khaledi, P.; Smith, C.; Siskind, D.; Gratten, J.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Mater Research Institute, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, Queensland, Australia
data.abstract: Background: About one-third of individuals with schizophrenia do not respond to first-line antipsychotics. Clozapine has superior efficacy for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS), yet remains underutilised partly due to a 1% risk of potentially fatal clozapine-induced neutropenia (CIN). However, the biological mechanisms underlying CIN remain poorly understood. Methods: We recruited six individuals with TRS who had previously received clozapine: three who ceased clozapine following CIN and three who stopped for reasons unrelated to CIN. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells were collected and cultured in vitro under three conditions: untreated, clozapine alone, or clozapine with its two major metabolites. Single nucleus RNA sequencing was performed to profile the cellular transcriptomic landscape following exposure to clozapine and its metabolites. Results: After quality control, 59,313 cells spanning 26 distinct clusters were retained. Multiple cell type-specific genes were differentially expressed in TRS with CIN, or in response to clozapine exposure in TRS donors with CIN (but not in those without CIN), after adjusting for age, sex and smoking status. We also identified a CIN-associated co-expression module in naive CD4 T cells that was driven by the transcription factor SREBF1, and robust evidence for differential cell-cell communication involving seven intercellular ligand-receptor pairs. There was limited evidence that clozapine-related metabolites contributed to these transcriptional changes. Conclusions: Our findings provide novel insights into cell type-specific transcriptional changes associated with CIN status and/or clozapine exposure in TRS with CIN. With replication in larger, independent cohorts, this work may contribute to the future development of predictive biomarkers for CIN and safer therapeutic strategies for TRS.

data.title: Preprint: Clinical Prediction Model Performance Metrics Cluster at Arbitrary Thresholds and are Incorrectly Reported in High-Ranking Journals: An Observational Meta-Research Study
data.authors: Gibson, A. D.; Borg, D. N.; White, N. M.; Barnett, A.
data.abstract: Background Previous research has shown that clinical prediction models have likely been 'hacked' to meet arbitrary performance thresholds. However, this work only assessed abstracts, could not identify models with a perfect AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) of 1, and did not examine other performance metrics. Methods We collected data from full texts and validated a large language model to extract data from a random sample of Q1 journal articles for 2025. We examined if hacking occurred in the AUC value, sensitivity and specificity, and checked if articles correctly reported the AUC value from corresponding receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. Results We identified 2,001 prediction model articles that reported 15,656 AUC values. We found a striking excess of results near perfect prediction and at multiples of five and ten for the AUC, sensitivity and specificity, indicating likely manipulated data, methods or publication bias. Around 1 in 40 AUC values were reported outside of their confidence intervals, and around 1 in 8 ROC curves did not match their reported AUC value. Conclusion We have shown that not only the AUC value, but the sensitivity and specificity are being hacked, likely to help the authors publish their paper at the cost of evidence for practice. Excess models that are not representative of their true performance may misguide clinicians, distort the literature, and make it harder to find prediction models that are useful for practice.

data.title: Preprint: Using Vision and Large Language Models for Psychological Intervention Competency Assessment: A Pilot Study of Agreement with Clinician Ratings
data.authors: Liu, Y.; Leever, W.; Stanco, M.; Shook, Z.; Addico, P.; Gleeson, S.; Nugroho, F.; Varney, G.; Youngstrom, E.; Sezgin, E.
data.abstract: Introduction: Supervision in psychological intervention training is limited by the time needed to evaluate simulated sessions. We tested a Vision Language Model (VLM) and Large Language Model (LLM) pipeline that assesses competency from verbal and nonverbal communication. Method: Gemini-3.1-Pro was used to annotate behaviors in 25 simulated therapy videos and incorporate them into transcripts, and ChatGPT-6.1-Sol rated them against the ENACT scale. Two clinicians verified VLM-identified behaviors and four independently rated each video. Agreement was estimated with Gwet's AC1 and ICC. Results: Of 1,558 VLM-identified behaviors, 70% were confirmed by both clinicians and 93% by at least one. AI-clinician agreement on therapeutic behavior attributes (AC1=0.73, 95% CI 0.70-0.76) approached between-clinician agreement (0.75, 0.72-0.78). AI-clinician ICCs on therapeutic domain levels (median 0.57) were modestly lower than between-clinician ICCs (0.67). Discussion: The pipeline agreed with clinicians nearly as well as clinicians agreed with each other and shows promise as a supplementary evaluator in therapist training.

data.title: Preprint: Impact of a hospital digital coordination centre on patient flow in a large tertiary centre
data.authors: Davey, B.; Shaw, L.; Plumb, S.; Aranha, S.; Fazio, T.; Spelman, T.; Chapman, W.; Astbury, B.; Gazarek, J.; Steel, P. A. D.; Capurro, D.; Cornell, P. Y.
data.author_corresponding_institution: University of Melbourne, Centre for Digital Transformation of Health
data.abstract: Hospitals globally are under increasing strain due to rising demand and constrained capacity. This interrupted-time-series study evaluates the impact of a digital coordination centre, implemented on August 28th of 2023, where a multidisciplinary operational team (comprising data scientists, patient flow managers, facilities managers, patient transport and nursing staff, for example) use real-time data dashboards showing measures of emergency department (ED) crowding and inpatient utilisation to optimise patient flow in an Australian metropolitan tertiary hospital. Analysis of 191,415 emergency department arrivals admitted to acute care and 187,783 acute inpatient episodes between July 2020 and July 2025 showed substantial improvements in measures of patient flow: 33% decrease in ED length of stay, 73% increase in hospital admissions from the ED within four hours of arrival, 7% decrease in inpatient length of stay, and 5% increase in discharges completed before noon. These changes coincided with a broader programme of organisational and operational reform, of which the DCC was a central integrating component. Hence, the findings support digitally enabled coordination centres as an effective contribution the overall strategy for improving hospital operational efficiency.

data.title: Preprint: Structural and Social Disadvantage and Post-Migration HIV Vulnerability among African, Caribbean, and Black Communities in Ontario
data.authors: Tharao, W.; Nyoni, T.; Amoako, E.; Fombang, D. N. T.; Perryman, A.; Daftary, A.; Ndungu, M.; MacNeily, J.; Bullock, S.; Blot, S.; Pierre-Pierre, V.; Loutfy, M.; Kaul, R.; Tan, D.; Rachlis, A.; Cooper, C.; Salit, I.; Luyombya, H.; Ryan, S. T.; Calzavara, L.; Team, M. S.
data.author_corresponding_institution: School of Social Work, Faculty of Health, Dalhousie University, Halifax, NS, Canada
data.abstract: Background. African, Caribbean, and Black (ACB) communities in Canada experience a disproportionate burden of HIV, and a considerable share of infections among ACB immigrants is acquired after arrival in Canada. Yet how ACB people themselves understand the structural circumstances surrounding post-migration acquisition remains underexamined. This study asked how intersecting structural and social disadvantages shape post-migration HIV vulnerability among ACB communities in Ontario. Methods. We conducted an interpretive secondary thematic analysis of 44 in-depth interviews from the MSAFIRI Study, read through intersectionality and structural-vulnerability lenses. Interviews were coded inductively and deductively by two analysts, with consensus adjudication and community review of the thematic structure. Results. Five structural conditions organized participants accounts: racism as a structural condition of settlement; immigration precarity and the work of settling alone; economic precarity, including insecure work, poverty, and unstable housing; ruptured kin networks and isolation under migration; and gendered violence and homophobia. These conditions compounded one another, so that disadvantage in one domain deepened vulnerability in another. Conclusion. Post-migration HIV vulnerability among ACB communities is produced by intersecting structural disadvantages encountered in the receiving country context. Equitable HIV prevention requires structural and community-led responses that address immigration precarity, economic and housing insecurity, gendered violence, homophobia, and anti-Black racism, alongside biomedical and individual-level prevention. Keywords: HIV; African, Caribbean, and Black communities; migration; structural vulnerability; intersectionality; social determinants of health; Canada

data.title: Preprint: Generation-time distortion is an emergent property of epidemic control
data.authors: Parag, K. V.; De Leenheer, P.; Pates, R.
data.abstract: We find that a vast space of public health interventions necessarily reshape the intervals between successive infections, known as generation times, for directly-transmitted infectious diseases (e.g., COVID-19, Ebola virus, influenza). While some studies have connected specific interventions (e.g., contact-tracing, isolation) to shifted generation times, most epidemiological analyses assume these intervals are stationary. We reveal that this assumption is substantially more fragile than previously recognised. We develop a universal microscopic representation for all intervention mechanisms that reduce individual-level infectiousness and establish generation-time reshaping as a fundamental macroscopic feature of those interventions, emerging at the population level. By constraining the topology of our representation to reflect specific mechanisms, we explain and unify previous studies as well as predict generation-time phenomena yet to be observed. We further show that neglecting generation-time reshaping can under- or over-estimate intervention effectiveness and disease control- lability by 100%, under realistic parameter settings. A stringent intervention can even produce no estimated transmissibility difference. Generation-time distortion causes unavoidable and underrated biases that can severely limit model-driven public health policy and pandemic preparedness.

data.title: Preprint: Perioperative non-invasive brain stimulation for the prevention of postoperative delirium: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
data.authors: Wang, H.; Du, L.; Li, D.; Zhang, A.; Huang, Y.; Liu, X.; Shu, J.; Zhang, H.; Zou, J.; Pan, H.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Anesthesiology, Sichuan Clinical Research Center for Cancer, Sichuan Cancer Hospital & Institute, Sichuan Cancer Center, University of Electronic
data.abstract: Background: Postoperative delirium is a common perioperative complication. Early randomised trials suggested that non-invasive brain stimulation may reduce postoperative delirium, whereas the recent MODEST trial found no preventive benefit. We synthesised the randomised evidence for perioperative non-invasive brain stimulation. Methods: We searched eight bibliographic databases and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to 30 September 2026 for randomised controlled trials of perioperative non-invasive brain stimulation in adults undergoing surgery. The primary outcome was postoperative delirium. Random-effects meta-analyses estimated risk ratios (RRs), mean differences, or standardised mean differences. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and certainty of evidence using GRADE. Results: Nine trials contributed data from 1451 participants. Postoperative delirium occurred in 72 of 750 participants receiving active stimulation and 166 of 701 controls (RR 0.41, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.31-0.56; I2=24.7%; moderate-certainty evidence). Estimates also favoured stimulation for hypoactive and hyperactive delirium, but not clearly for mixed delirium. Pain, anxiety, and sleep outcomes favoured stimulation but were highly heterogeneous and supported by very-low-certainty evidence. Length of hospital stay was not reduced. Adverse events could not be pooled because reporting was incomplete and inconsistent. Conclusions: Perioperative non-invasive brain stimulation may reduce postoperative delirium, but the evidence does not establish a class effect or support routine clinical use. Geographical concentration, methodological concerns, heterogeneous stimulation protocols, and discordance with the MODEST trial warrant independent multicentre sham-controlled trials. PROSPERO registration: CRD420261522168 Keywords: meta-analysis; non-invasive brain stimulation; perioperative neurocognitive disorders; postoperative delirium; transcranial direct current stimulation; transcranial magnetic stimulation

Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and certainty of evidence using GRADE. Results: Nine trials contributed data from 1451 participants. Postoperative delirium occurred in 72 of 750 participants receiving active stimulation and 166 of 701 controls (RR 0.41, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.31-0.56; I2=24.7%; moderate-certainty evidence). Estimates also favoured stimulation for hypoactive and hyperactive delirium, but not clearly for mixed delirium. Pain, anxiety, and sleep outcomes favoured stimulation but were highly heterogeneous and supported by very-low-certainty evidence. Length of hospital stay was not reduced. Adverse events could not be pooled because reporting was incomplete and inconsistent. Conclusions: Perioperative non-invasive brain stimulation may reduce postoperative delirium, but the evidence does not establish a class effect or support routine clinical use. Geographical concentration, methodological concerns, heterogeneous stimulation protocols, and discordance with the MODEST trial warrant independent multicentre sham-controlled trials. data.title: Preprint: Cryopreserved Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells Recover Mitochondrial Function Following Overnight Culture Revealed by High-Resolution Respirometry
data.authors: 'Atiola, R.; Puliuvea, C.; Netzler, N.; Merry, T.; Shepherd, P. R.; Hedges, C.; Hickey, T.; Vailahi, G.
data.abstract: Abstract Background: High resolution respirometry of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) is widely used to assess mitochondrial function, but reliance on freshly isolated cells limits flexibility and sample batching. The impact of cryopreservation and post-thaw handling on PBMC mitochondrial respiration remains incompletely defined. Methods: PBMCs from healthy young adults were analysed under three conditions: freshly isolated, cryopreserved and directly thawed, and cryopreserved followed by overnight recovery in supplemented culture medium. Mitochondrial respiration was assessed using an Oroboros O2k high-resolution respirometer following plasma membrane permeabilisation and a substrate uncoupler inhibitor titration protocol. Respiration parameters included leak, oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), maximal uncoupled respiration, and non-mitochondrial oxygen consumption. Results: Directly thawed PBMCs exhibited reduced ATP-coupled and maximal respiratory flux compared with fresh cells, indicating acute cryopreservation-induced mitochondrial suppression. In contrast, PBMCs undergoing overnight recovery showed substantial restoration of mitochondrial function, with OXPHOS and uncoupled respiration closely approximating those of fresh cells. Cell viability was comparable across conditions. Conclusion: Cryopreserved PBMCs can be reliably used for mitochondrial respirometry when an overnight recovery step is included. This approach enables sample storage, batching, and broader application in large-scale and retrospective human studies.
